lead: The throttle position sensor tells the engine control unit (ECU) how far the driver has pressed the accelerator. Temperature sensors tell the ECU how hot the engine coolant, intake air, battery and cabin are. These signals set fuel, ignition, idle speed and climate comfort. A throttle position sensor is a position sensor with a safety check; a temperature sensor is usually a negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor in a voltage divider. Both reach the ECU through an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) and a calibration table. This chapter shows the circuits, the non-linearity traps and the redundancy checks that keep the readings trustworthy.
prereq: You need: sensor basics and signal conditioning for voltage dividers and ADC counts, and Hall, reluctance and optical sensors for contactless position sensing.

blocks.text: The throttle plate controls air into a petrol engine. The throttle position sensor (TPS) converts plate angle into a voltage. The ECU uses it for idle control, acceleration enrichment, gear shift decisions and cruise control. A simple TPS is a potentiometer: a resistive track fed with a stable 5 V reference, and a wiper driven by the throttle shaft. The wiper voltage rises with opening. Many units have two tracks with opposite slopes; the ECU checks that their sum stays constant, so a broken wiper or short is detected.

blocks.where: V<sub>TPS</sub> is the wiper voltage in V; V₀ is the voltage at closed throttle in V; k is the slope in V per % throttle; θ is throttle opening in %.

blocks.text: A contactless TPS uses a Hall element or an inductive coil. A magnet turns with the throttle shaft and the output changes without rubbing. It lasts longer and has no wiper noise. Some systems call it a throttle angle sensor. The accelerator pedal has two independent position sensors, often with different slopes or a fixed ratio. The ECU compares them: if they disagree by more than a small window, it limits engine power and sets a fault code.

items: Read both tracks through separate ADC channels.
Check 0.5 V to 4.5 V range at ignition on.
Check track sum or ratio at each angle.
I<sub>f</sub> plausible, use a calibrated table for throttle %.
I<sub>f</sub> not, use a limp-home value and store a fault code.

blocks.text: Older systems add a closed-throttle idle switch and a wide-open-throttle (WOT) switch. The idle switch confirms 0% for idle speed control; the WOT switch signals maximum load for enrichment. A switch is a yes/no contact, not a measured angle.

Engine coolant temperature (ECT) and intake air temperature (IAT) sensors are negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistors. Their resistance falls as temperature rises. A typical circuit puts the thermistor to ground and a fixed pull-up resistor to a clean 5 V reference. The junction voltage goes to the ADC. With this arrangement the voltage falls as temperature rises. The same 5 V usually feeds the ADC reference, so a slow drift in it cancels (the reading is ratiometric); a bad ground or a sensor fed from a different supply does not cancel.

V<sub>out</sub> is the divider voltage in V; V<sub>ref</sub> is the sensor supply in V; R<sub>pull</sub> is the fixed resistor in Ω; R<sub>NTC</sub> is the thermistor resistance in Ω at the measured temperature.

The NTC curve is not a straight line. A two-point linear conversion is wrong in the middle. The ECU stores a table of resistance or voltage against temperature, or evaluates the Steinhart-Hart equation. The table has more points near cold starts, where fuel correction matters. IAT corrects air density; ECT corrects fuel and ignition during warm-up and controls the radiator fan. Battery thermal sensors use the same thermistor idea to protect charging and traction batteries.
1/T = A + B ln R + C (ln R)³
blocks.where: T is absolute temperature in K; R is thermistor resistance in Ω; A, B and C are constants for that thermistor.

blocks.text: A thermistor is a resistor, not a thermocouple. It needs a divider and an ADC. The pull-up resistor value sets the voltage range. Choose it so the ADC uses most of its range over the expected temperature span. Check the connector and ground: a high-resistance ground or connector adds an offset, so compare the divider voltage with the table before replacing the sensor.

Climate control needs more than one temperature. A cabin temperature sensor with a small fan samples the air near the dash. An outside temperature sensor gives ambient. A sun-load sensor on the dash measures solar heating. A humidity sensor, often capacitive, measures water vapour in the cabin air. An air-quality sensor detects reducing gases or particles and selects recirculation. The climate ECU combines these signals with the target temperature and blower status to drive air blend doors and the compressor. The flap and blend-door motors are covered in solenoids, relays and stepper motors.

The same thermal sensing appears in the battery pack. Several NTC thermistors report module temperature to the battery management system (BMS). The BMS compares them and reduces charging power if one is hot. Humidity sensing also protects electronics: condensation can short connectors. Air-quality signals are slow and noisy, so the ECU filters them and uses hysteresis, a small dead band, before changing recirculation.

figure.caption: Left: the TPS line of the first worked example, 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open, with 30 % at 1.70 V. Right: the coolant divider of the second example, computed from the thermistor equation: the voltage falls along a curve, from 4.133 V at −10 °C to 0.545 V at 90 °C, so the ECU needs a table.

spec.aria: Two graphs. Left: throttle position sensor voltage rising in a straight line from 0.5 volts at 0 per cent to 4.5 volts at 100 per cent, with 30 per cent marked at 1.70 volts. Right: NTC divider output falling along a curve with temperature, 4.133 volts at minus 10 degrees and 0.545 volts at 90 degrees.

examples.question: A throttle position sensor has a linear characteristic: 0.5 V at 0% throttle and 4.5 V at 100% throttle. The ECU uses a 10-bit ADC with 0 V → 0 and 5 V → 1023. Find (a) the TPS voltage at 30% throttle and (b) the ADC count for that voltage.
steps: ADC count = round(1023 × V<sub>TPS</sub> / 5 V) = round(1023 × 1.70 / 5) = round(347.82) = 348.
Full scale is 1023, not 1024, because a 10-bit ADC gives counts 0 to 1023.
examples.answer: At 30% throttle the TPS voltage is 1.70 V and the 10-bit ADC count is 348.
examples.check:
v0=0.5
v100=4.5
throttle=30
k=(v100-v0)/100
v=v0+k*throttle
count=round(1023*v/5)
print(f"{v:.2f}")
print(count)

examples.question: An NTC coolant sensor has R = 2.2 kΩ at 25 °C and B = 3500 K. It sits from the ECU input to ground with a 2.2 kΩ pull-up to 5 V, read by a 10-bit ADC. Using R = R<sub>25</sub> exp[B (1/T − 1/298.15)], find the resistance, the divider voltage and the ADC count at 90 °C and at −10 °C.
steps: Check: the hot reading uses only 111 counts, so one count near 90 °C is worth about 0.4 °C. That is why many ECUs switch in a second, smaller pull-up once the engine is warm.
examples.answer: 90 °C: 269 Ω, 0.545 V, count 111. −10 °C: 10.48 kΩ, 4.133 V, count 846. The voltage falls as the coolant warms.

traps: Do not treat an NTC thermistor as linear. A straight line through two temperatures gives large errors in between.
The ADC count uses full scale 1023 for 10 bits, not 1024. A 5 V reference gives count = round(1023 × V / 5).
TPS redundancy is not two identical signals. The tracks often have opposite slopes or a fixed ratio; the ECU checks agreement, not equality.
A bad sensor ground or 5 V reference shifts TPS and temperature readings together. Check supply and ground before replacing the sensor.
Idle and WOT switches are not analog angle sensors. They only confirm endpoints and cannot replace the TPS curve.

quiz.q: What does a TPS measure, and what does the ECU use it for?
quiz.a: It measures the throttle plate angle. The ECU uses it for idle control, acceleration enrichment, gear-shift decisions and cruise control; the accelerator pedal has its own pair of sensors.

quiz.q: What is an NTC thermistor? How does its resistance change with temperature?
quiz.a: A negative temperature coefficient thermistor is a resistor whose resistance falls as temperature rises.

quiz.q: Why does a TPS often have two tracks? How does the ECU use them?
quiz.a: For safety. The ECU compares the two signals, often a sum or ratio, and limits power if they disagree.

quiz.q: A TPS has 0.5 V at 0% and 4.5 V at 100%. Find the voltage at 60% and the 10-bit ADC count for a 0–5 V ADC.
The ECT reads correctly when the engine is cold but about 20 °C too cold when the engine is hot. Give two possible causes and one test.
quiz.a: A resistance in series with the thermistor: a corroded connector or a high-resistance sensor ground. When hot the NTC is only a few hundred ohms, so an extra 100 Ω raises the divider voltage a lot and the ECU reads colder; when cold the NTC is several kilohms and the same 100 Ω hardly shows. Test: unplug the sensor, measure its resistance and the loom resistance to the ECU pin, and compare with the table.

quiz.q: Why is a table or the Steinhart-Hart equation used for an NTC instead of a single slope?
quiz.a: Because the resistance-temperature curve is nonlinear. A table or equation gives accurate temperature over the full range.

quiz.q: A divider has V<sub>ref</sub> = 5 V, R<sub>pull</sub> = 1.0 kΩ and R<sub>NTC</sub> = 1.0 kΩ. Find V<sub>out</sub> and the 10-bit ADC count.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production throttle bodies now use contactless sensors with digital outputs such as SENT or PSI5, and the ECU checks them with model-based plausibility. Battery packs use chains of NTC thermistors and sometimes fibre-optic temperature sensing. Cabin comfort systems combine humidity, sun load and air quality with CO₂ sensing to save energy in electric vehicles. Search next for 'SENT protocol', 'Steinhart-Hart thermistor linearisation' and 'battery thermal management sensors'.
